title: IRR17 & IR(ME)R17: the law and its roles
blurb: The two sets of UK regulations behind every dental X-ray: who they protect, the RPA and RPS, local rules, and the four IR(ME)R duty holders.
question: On your first week in a new practice, the practice manager asks you to read the local rules and sign to say you understand them. Later the dentist asks you to position the receptor and press the exposure button. Which regulations cover each of these, and what must be in place before you can act as an operator?

teach.body: Dental radiography in the UK is governed by two sets of regulations. The Ionising Radiations Regulations 2017 (IRR17) protect workers and the public, and are enforced by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE). The Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017 (IR(ME)R 2017) protect patients, plus carers and comforters who knowingly support them. A simple way to remember it: IRR17 is about the people taking the X-ray and those nearby; IR(ME)R is about the person having it, the ME in the middle.

teach.h: Who and what each set covers
teach.caption: The employer carries the legal responsibility under both sets and cannot delegate it.

teach.body: Under IRR17 the employer must register with the HSE before using X-ray equipment, carry out a radiation risk assessment, and consult a Radiation Protection Adviser (RPA): an external expert who advises on room layout, the controlled area, local rules, pregnant staff and training. Where a controlled area exists, the employer must appoint a Radiation Protection Supervisor (RPS) in writing, usually a dentist, to make sure the local rules are followed day to day. Legal responsibility still stays with the employer.

rows.label: Name(s) of the Radiation Protection Supervisor
Where the controlled area is and when it exists
Key working instructions to restrict exposure
Arrangements for access to the controlled area
Summary of contingency plans for foreseeable accidents

teach.note: Local rules must be in writing, brought to the attention of everyone affected and readily accessible where X-ray equipment is used. Annual review is recommended.

head: Duty holder
Responsibility
Usually
rows: Written procedures, entitles and trains staff
teach.caption: A Medical Physics Expert (MPE) advises the employer on optimisation and quality assurance. One person can hold several roles: a dentist is often referrer, practitioner and operator.

teach.body: No exposure can happen until an IR(ME)R practitioner has justified it: decided that the diagnostic benefit outweighs the radiation risk. They weigh up previous radiographs, the history and examination, the patient's age and any alternative without X-rays. The decision is recorded as an authorisation. There is no justification for routine radiographs of new patients without a clinical examination. As an operator, you must only expose once you know the exposure has been justified.

teach.h: The safe sequence for every exposure

steps.label: Identify the patient
steps.sub: Ask for name, address and date of birth

teach.caption: Rushing or skipping the identity and positioning checks is a common cause of IR(ME)R incidents such as the wrong patient or wrong tooth being X-rayed.

teach.body: An operator is anyone who carries out a practical part of an exposure: identifying the patient, positioning the receptor, patient and tubehead, setting the exposure, pressing the button, processing images, or clinical evaluation. A dental nurse can be an operator, but only once the employer has trained them for that task, recorded the training and formally entitled them. Entitlement is what makes it lawful. Being asked by a dentist is not enough on its own. Taking radiographs as a dental nurse is an additional skill requiring further training.

teach.h: Can I press the exposure button?

teach.text: Don't mix up the advisers: the RPA (IRR17) advises on protecting STAFF and the public; the MPE (IR(ME)R) advises on PATIENT dose and quality. The RPS supervises the local rules in the practice.

items: IRR17 protects staff and public (HSE); IR(ME)R 2017 protects patients.
IRR17: register with HSE, risk assessment, consult RPA, appoint RPS in writing, local rules, controlled area.
IR(ME)R duty holders: employer, referrer, practitioner (justifies), operator (practical tasks).
Only a trained and entitled operator may expose; justification is always the first check.

summary: You can now tell IRR17 from IR(ME)R 2017, explain the roles of the employer, RPA, RPS and MPE, list what the local rules must contain, name the four IR(ME)R duty holders, and follow the safe sequence from identification to evaluation.

A.q: Which regulations are mainly concerned with protecting PATIENTS undergoing dental radiography?
A.why: IR(ME)R 2017 covers medical exposures, so it protects patients (and carers and comforters).

whyNot.0: IRR17 protects workers and members of the public, not patients.
whyNot.1: COSHH covers hazardous substances such as chemicals, not radiation.
whyNot.3: RIDDOR covers reporting of workplace injuries and dangerous occurrences.

A.q: Under IR(ME)R 2017, whose main job is to JUSTIFY an exposure?
A.why: The IR(ME)R practitioner takes responsibility for the exposure; their primary function is justification.

whyNot.0: The operator carries out practical tasks such as positioning and exposing.
whyNot.2: The referrer supplies the clinical information the practitioner needs.
whyNot.3: The RPS is an IRR17 role supervising the local rules, not justifying exposures.

A.q: A new nurse asks where the local rules should be kept. Which answer is correct?
options: Locked in the practice manager's office
Kept only by the RPA off site
Readily available where X-rays are used
A.why: IRR17 requires local rules to be brought to staff's attention and readily accessible where the X-ray equipment is used.

whyNot.0: Locking them away stops staff consulting them when they need to.
whyNot.1: The RPA helps draft them, but the practice must keep them accessible.
whyNot.2: Local rules are working instructions for staff, not patient information.

B.q: Who must the employer appoint in writing wherever a controlled area exists?
options: A Health and Safety Executive officer
B.why: IRR17 requires an RPS to be appointed in writing wherever there is a controlled area, to supervise adherence to the local rules.

whyNot.1: The MPE is an IR(ME)R role advising on patient dose and QA.
whyNot.2: The HSE is the regulator; the employer doesn't appoint its officers.
whyNot.3: The RPA must be consulted, but the written in-house appointment for the controlled area is the RPS.

B.q: A dental nurse has been asked to take a bitewing for the first time. What makes it lawful for them to act as an operator?
options: Having watched the dentist do it often
B.why: Under IR(ME)R, operators must be adequately trained for each task and entitled by the employer through written procedures.

whyNot.0: Registration alone does not cover radiography; it is an additional skill needing training.
whyNot.1: A dentist's request does not replace training and formal entitlement.
whyNot.3: Observation is not training, and it gives no entitlement.

B.q: Which of these must the local rules always contain?
B.why: IRR17 guidance says local rules must always name the Radiation Protection Supervisor(s).

whyNot.0: Patient doses are recorded in clinical records, not local rules.
whyNot.2: GDC numbers are not part of the local rules.
whyNot.3: Cost has nothing to do with radiation protection instructions.

C.q: Which of these must be confirmed before any setting up or positioning for a radiograph begins?
options: Placing the receptor holder in the mouth
C.why: Every exposure must be justified by an IR(ME)R practitioner before anything else happens; positive patient ID goes alongside it.

whyNot.0: Exposure settings come later, once the exposure is justified and the patient positioned.
whyNot.1: Positioning only happens after the exposure is confirmed as justified.
whyNot.3: The warning light shows the equipment is ready; it is not a justification check.

C.q: Which body enforces IRR17 in dental practices in Great Britain?
C.why: IRR17 is health and safety law, enforced by the HSE, with which the employer must register before using X-ray equipment.

whyNot.1: The GDC regulates dental professionals, not radiation safety law.
whyNot.2: NHS England commissions dental services but does not enforce IRR17.
whyNot.3: Planning offices have no role in radiation protection.

C.q: An X-ray is taken of the wrong patient because the nurse didn't check identity. Which part of the safe sequence was missed?
C.why: Positive identification, asking the patient for name, address and date of birth, prevents wrong-patient exposures.

whyNot.0: Evaluation comes after the exposure and cannot prevent this error.
whyNot.1: Explaining the procedure helps cooperation but does not confirm who the patient is.
whyNot.2: Exposure settings affect image quality, not which patient is exposed.

reteach.title: A building site analogy
reteach.question: Imagine a building site with a crane. Who keeps the workers safe, and who makes sure the crane only lifts what it should?

blocks.body: IRR17 is the site safety rulebook: hard-hat zones (the controlled area), a safety consultant (the RPA), a site supervisor who enforces the rules (the RPS) and a notice board of rules (local rules). IR(ME)R is about the load itself, here the patient: someone orders the lift (referrer), an engineer decides it is necessary and safe (practitioner), and a trained, licensed crane driver does it (operator). The site owner (employer) is responsible for everything.

blocks.text: The PRACTITIONER justifies; the OPERATOR does. A dental nurse doesn't act as the IR(ME)R practitioner, but can be an operator once trained and entitled.

explain.body: IRR17 protects staff and the public and is enforced by the HSE. IR(ME)R 2017 protects patients and carers or comforters. The employer is responsible under both.

test.q: Which is an IRR17 requirement rather than an IR(ME)R one?
test.why: Local rules are an IRR17 requirement to restrict exposure of staff and others in the controlled area.

whyNot.0: Justification is the core IR(ME)R principle.
whyNot.2: Clinical evaluation is an IR(ME)R requirement for each exposure.
whyNot.3: Entitling referrers is part of the IR(ME)R employer's procedures.

explain.body: The RPA is an external expert the employer must consult on radiation protection. The RPS is appointed in writing, usually from within the practice, to supervise the local rules wherever a controlled area exists.

test.q: Which statement about the RPS is correct?
options: They take over the employer's legal duty
They must be an external physicist
They supervise adherence to local rules
test.why: The RPS supervises day-to-day compliance with the local rules; legal responsibility stays with the employer.

whyNot.0: Legal responsibility cannot be passed from the employer.
whyNot.1: The RPS is usually a member of practice staff; the RPA is the external expert.
whyNot.3: Justification is the IR(ME)R practitioner's job.

explain.body: Employer: procedures and entitlement. Referrer: clinical information. IR(ME)R practitioner: justification. Operator: practical tasks. The MPE advises on patient dose and QA.

test.q: A dental nurse processes phosphor plates after an exposure. Which duty holder role are they performing?
test.why: Processing images is a practical aspect of an exposure, so it is an operator function.

whyNot.0: The referrer requests the exposure and supplies clinical information.
whyNot.1: The employer sets procedures and entitles staff.

explain.body: Identify the patient positively, confirm the exposure is justified, explain, position, expose from outside the controlled area, then check image quality and make sure it is clinically evaluated and recorded.

test.q: Which order is correct for taking a radiograph?
test.why: You identify the patient, confirm justification, position, then expose; evaluation follows.

whyNot.0: Positioning before identification risks X-raying the wrong person.
whyNot.1: Exposing before identifying and positioning is unsafe.
whyNot.2: Identification must happen before the exposure, not after.
